//: What a framework stopped offering, grouped by the thing it offered rather than by the types that named it.
//1: The unit of decision is the feature. On nopCommerce 3.90, forty-four types modern .NET does not have come to six questions, and two attributes of a seventh accounted for 596 calls on their own.
//2: Options are what a person chooses between, written plainly and checkable. None of them is a recommendation: which one is right depends on things that are not in the code, which is the whole reason this file exists.

Microsoft.AspNet.Mvc.name: The request context
Microsoft.AspNet.Mvc.was: System.Web wrapped the request in a family of abstract base classes so that code could be tested against them, and passed one around as the ambient state of the request.
Microsoft.AspNet.Mvc.now: ASP.NET Core has HttpContext and its parts, injected rather than ambient, with different names and a different shape. An uploaded file is IFormFile, cookies are IRequestCookieCollection, and there is no HttpException.
options: Move the code onto the new types directly. Shortest where the class already receives the context as an argument.
Put an interface of your own in front of what you actually use, and implement it over the new types. Longest, and the only option that lets the old and the new code run side by side.
Push the context out of the class entirely and pass the values it reads. Turns a migration into a design change, which is sometimes the right trade and never a small one.

Microsoft.AspNet.Mvc.name: Bundling and minification
Microsoft.AspNet.Mvc.was: System.Web.Optimization combined and minified scripts and stylesheets at run time, from bundles declared in code.
Microsoft.AspNet.Mvc.now: Nothing in ASP.NET Core does this. The framework serves static files and expects the assets to have been built already.
options: Build the assets with the toolchain the front end already uses, and serve the output as static files.
Use a community package that reproduces the old behaviour, if the bundles are many and the front end has no build.
Serve the files unbundled. Defensible over HTTP/2, and it is a decision about latency rather than about code.

Microsoft.AspNet.Mvc.name: Display modes
Microsoft.AspNet.Mvc.was: MVC picked a different view file for a mobile browser, by matching a suffix on the file name.
Microsoft.AspNet.Mvc.now: Removed. ASP.NET Core selects views by name and by area, and knows nothing about the user agent.
options: Drop it and serve one responsive view, which is what most of these turn out to be.
Select the view yourself in the action, from whatever you were matching on.
Keep two views and route to them, if they are genuinely different pages rather than one page at two widths.

Microsoft.AspNet.Mvc.name: Model binding extensibility
Microsoft.AspNet.Mvc.was: Binding was extended by deriving from the default binder or replacing the metadata provider, both of which knew a great deal about the pipeline around them.
Microsoft.AspNet.Mvc.now: ASP.NET Core binds through IModelBinder and IModelBinderProvider, registered in options. The shape is similar and the base classes are not there to derive from.
options: Write the binder against the new interfaces. Usually smaller than the original, because the default no longer has to be reimplemented around it.
Check first whether the framework now does it. Several of these existed to bind types that bind on their own today.

Microsoft.AspNet.Mvc.name: Areas
Microsoft.AspNet.Mvc.was: An area registered itself by deriving from AreaRegistration, and the framework found it by scanning assemblies at startup.
Microsoft.AspNet.Mvc.now: Areas still exist and there is nothing to register: a controller carries [Area] and routes name it.
options: Delete the registration classes and put [Area] on the controllers.
Ask first whether the areas earn their keep, because the routing they were working around is gone.

Microsoft.AspNet.Mvc.name: Pipeline internals
Microsoft.AspNet.Mvc.was: Code that reached into how MVC found controllers, resolved views or handled the application lifetime. Global.asax is the usual entry point.
Microsoft.AspNet.Mvc.now: There is no equivalent, and that is deliberate: the pipeline is middleware you compose in Program.cs rather than handlers you replace.
options: Find what the code was working around and check whether the new pipeline does it already. Most of these predate features the framework grew.
Write it as middleware, which is where the behaviour belongs now.
Treat it as a rewrite of that concern, and price it as one. This is the group that genuinely costs.
